title: Snakebite
summary: Bitten by a snake (North America): stay calm, keep still, get to antivenom. No cutting, sucking, or tourniquets.
sources: Wilderness Medical Society Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Pitviper Envenomations in the United States and Canada
firstLine: Move away from the snake. Do not try to catch or kill it. A photo from a safe distance is enough. Call 911 or Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) if you can.

nodes.prompt: Any of these: trouble breathing, swelling of face or throat, fainting, or not responding?

nodes.title: Severe reaction
steps: If they carry an epinephrine auto-injector (EpiPen) and have face or throat swelling or hives, use it in the outer thigh.
Lay them down. If breathing is easier sitting up, let them sit.
Keep the bitten limb still.
Evacuate immediately by the fastest means available.

nodes.title: Snakebite first aid
steps: Keep the person calm and still. Walking or panicking spreads venom faster.
Remove rings, watches, bracelets, and tight clothing near the bite before swelling starts.
Keep the bitten limb still and roughly at heart level. A loose splint helps.
Mark the edge of any swelling with a pen and write the time. Update it every 15 minutes so medics can see how fast it spreads.
Wash the bite gently with water and cover it with a clean, loose dressing.
Note the time of the bite and what the snake looked like.
doNot: Do not cut the wound or try to suck out venom.
Do not use a tourniquet or tight bandage.
Do not put ice on it or soak it in water.
Do not give alcohol or pain medicines like aspirin or ibuprofen (they can worsen bleeding).
Do not use electric shock or snakebite "venom extractor" kits.

nodes.help: Antivenom is the only real treatment for a venomous bite, and it is only available in hospitals.

nodes.title: Get to a hospital
steps: Go now, even if they feel fine. Symptoms can be delayed for hours, especially with coral snake bites.
Carry or drive them if possible. If they must walk, go slowly and rest often.
Call ahead if you can so the hospital can get antivenom ready.
Bring the swelling time marks and your snake description or photo.

nodes.title: No hospital nearby
steps: Keep working toward help. Signal for rescue (radio, phone, PLB, signal mirror) as soon as possible.
Keep them resting, calm, limb still, and hydrated if they can swallow.
Keep marking swelling every 15 minutes.
Watch for spreading swelling, bleeding from gums or nose, vomiting, numbness, drooping eyelids, trouble swallowing or breathing. Any of these means they need antivenom urgently.
Many bites are "dry" (no venom). If there is no pain, swelling, or other symptoms after 8 to 12 hours, serious envenomation is unlikely, but get them checked when you can.

nodes.title: Severe reaction - evacuate now
steps: This is life-threatening. Get them to a hospital by the fastest means available.
Watch breathing constantly. If it stops, start CPR.

nodes.title: Not breathing - start CPR
steps: Start CPR immediately and use an AED if available.
